output.title: Tool consolidation is a design constraint, not a rebuild
output.body:
If you run a small business, tool consolidation is not mainly a software question. It is a design constraint: keep the tools you already use, and add one thin automation layer only where a handoff is repeated, rule-based, and worth the extra moving part. Replacing every app usually creates more switching cost than it removes.

A practical test is simple. List the tools in one recurring workflow, then trace the manual handoffs between them: CRM, email, invoicing, documents, calendar, and so on. Mark the step that causes the most delay or error. If that handoff repeats weekly, touches two or more tools, and has a clear outcome, it is a candidate for a bounded workflow. If it is one-off, low-frequency, or in a scope Bareni currently keeps out of service, the manual route may still be the cheaper choice.

That scope matters. Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work, bulk cold-email automation, and scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows. Human approval also stays mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions. Customer-held accounts and the option to pause or modify the workflow are Bareni policy, not an absolute legal warranty.

So the next step is not a rebuild. It is to map one recurring handoff, check whether it is repeatable and rule-based, and decide whether consolidation reduces friction or just rearranges it. If it only rearranges it, leave the stack alone.
